title: Concentrations after repeated IV bolus doses

segs.text: Module six, objective two. Concentrations at any time after repeated I V bolus doses. An I V bolus puts the whole dose into the plasma at once, so each peak comes at the moment of dosing. One dose on its own gives C zero, the dose, D zero, divided by V D, the volume of distribution that relates the amount in the body to C p. Between doses the level falls by first order elimination with rate constant k, and the fraction of a dose still in the body one interval later is e to the minus k tau, tau being the time between doses. That leftover is what accumulates.

card.m: IV bolus: peak at the moment of dosing
fraction left after τ: e<sup>−kτ</sup>; TID → τ = 8 hr

segs.text: Why does the level settle where it does? At steady state the drug eliminated over one interval equals one dose, so the drop from peak to trough equals one dose's C zero. That drop is also the peak times the fraction lost over one interval, one minus e to the minus k tau, so the peak must be C zero divided by the fraction lost. A shorter interval loses a smaller fraction, so the peak has to climb higher before the loss matches one dose. A larger dose raises peak, trough and drop in proportion; the fraction lost holds only k and tau.

card.m: drop = C<sub>max</sub><sup>∞</sup>(1 − e<sup>−kτ</sup>) = C<sub>0</sub> → C<sub>max</sub><sup>∞</sup> = {{frac:C<sub>0</sub>|1 − e<sup>−kτ</sup>}}
τ shorter → fraction lost smaller → C<sub>max</sub><sup>∞</sup> higher
D<sub>0</sub> × 2 → peak, trough, drop × 2; fraction lost unchanged

segs.text: In symbols, C max at steady state equals C zero over one minus e to the minus k tau. One over one minus e to the minus k tau is the accumulation factor, r, which holds only k and tau; k times tau has no units. A shorter tau leaves more behind, so the bottom, one minus e to the minus k tau, is smaller and the peak larger. The bottom is always less than one, so C max at steady state must come out above C zero. C min at steady state is the peak carried down one full interval, C max times e to the minus k tau, so the trough comes at the end of the interval.

card.m: r = {{frac:1|1 − e<sup>−kτ</sup>}}; kτ has no units
τ shorter → e<sup>−kτ</sup> larger → bottom smaller → C<sub>max</sub><sup>∞</sup> larger
C<sub>min</sub><sup>∞</sup> = C<sub>max</sub><sup>∞</sup>e<sup>−kτ</sup>, at the end of τ

segs.text: Next, the average at steady state. The fall is exponential, steeper while the level is high, so the curve spends more of each interval at lower levels and the average sits below the midpoint of peak and trough. She said, I want you to realize that the average is not the max plus the min divided by two. C average at steady state equals F D zero over Cl T tau, where Cl T, the total clearance, the volume of plasma cleared per unit of time, equals V D times k. F, the fraction of the dose reaching the circulation, is one for I V dosing. The dose is on top, so a larger dose raises the average; a longer tau or a larger clearance, underneath, lowers it.

card.m: exponential fall → more time at low levels → C<sub>avg</sub><sup>∞</sup> below {{frac:max + min|2}}
D<sub>0</sub> larger → C<sub>avg</sub><sup>∞</sup> larger; τ or Cl<sub>T</sub> larger → C<sub>avg</sub><sup>∞</sup> smaller; no e<sup>−kτ</sup>, no r

segs.text: Her Example one: an antibiotic with a half life of about four hours and a V D of twenty five percent of body weight is given at ten milligrams per kilogram every eight hours by I V bolus to a sixty five kilogram female. She asks the maximum, minimum and average at steady state, which the three steady state lines give. Dose and volume go on the same basis first, so V D is zero point two five liters per kilogram and C zero is forty milligrams per liter. From the half life, a quarter of each dose is left after one interval.

card.m: t<sub>½</sub> 4 hr, V<sub>D</sub> 25% of body weight, 10 mg/kg every 8 hr, 65 kg
V<sub>D</sub> = 0.25 L/kg; C<sub>0</sub> = {{frac:10 mg/kg|0.25 L/kg}} = 40 mg/L
or per patient: {{frac:650 mg|16.25 L}} = 40 mg/L

segs.text: The steady state peak is fifty three point three milligrams per liter, above the first dose peak of forty, as her check requires. She said, if you got a value less than forty milligrams per liter, you've done something wrong. The trough, a quarter of the peak, is thirteen point three milligrams per liter, and the gap is forty, one dose's C zero. The average is twenty eight point nine milligrams per liter, below the midpoint of thirty three point three, as the exponential fall predicts.

Before steady state, a dose number, n, tracks the climb. With f the fraction left after one interval, just after dose n the body holds one plus f plus f squared, up to f to the n minus one, doses: the build up. In symbols, C p equals D zero over V D, times the build up, one minus e to the minus n k tau over one minus e to the minus k tau, times e to the minus k t, with t the time since dose n, not since the first dose. As n grows, e to the minus n k tau shrinks toward zero, the build up becomes r, and this becomes the steady state line.

card.m: 1 + f + f<sup>2</sup> + ... + f<sup>n−1</sup> = {{frac:1 − f<sup>n</sup>|1 − f}}, f = e<sup>−kτ</sup>

segs.text: Her Example two asks the level three hours after the second dose of the same regimen. Two doses is not steady state, so the n dose line answers it, with n equal to two and t equal to three hours. The build up after two doses is one point two five, so the second peak is fifty milligrams per liter, as superposition gave in objective one. Three hours of decline from there leaves twenty nine point seven milligrams per liter.

Within a steady state interval, and after the last dose, C p is C max at steady state times e to the minus k t; she prefers this route to searching the sheet. In her final review poll, with three hundred milligrams every twelve hours, a four hour half life and a V D of sixteen liters, the key is twenty one point four milligrams per liter, while eighteen point seven is the first dose C zero, the answer without accumulation. A review item asks when the minimum occurs: at the end of the dosing interval, not in three to five half lives, which is the time to steady state. T I D, three times a day, must become a tau of eight hours.

card.m: C<sub>p</sub> = C<sub>max</sub><sup>∞</sup>e<sup>−kt</sup>, t since the last dose
300 mg every 12 hr, t<sub>½</sub> 4 hr, V<sub>D</sub> 16 L: C<sub>0</sub> = 18.75 mg/L
C<sub>min</sub><sup>∞</sup>: end of τ, not 3 to 5 t<sub>½</sub>
TID → τ = 8 hr; dose and V<sub>D</sub> on the same basis
